title: School Dormitory or Your Own Apartment? The Real Trade-offs in Year One
summary: This is usually framed as a price comparison. It is really a timing problem: the dormitory decision closes before you land, and renting is not available on day one.
body_html:
The comparison everyone makes is rent against rent. That is the least useful way to look at it, because the two options are not available at the same time.

By the time you could sign a lease, the dormitory decision has already been made and paid for. So the honest framing is not dormitory versus apartment. It is dormitory first and apartment later, or apartment from the start with a gap you have to cover somehow.

The dormitory decision closes before you arrive

One group publishes its allocation sequence in enough detail to see the problem. [source:2]

You are asked whether you want a dormitory after passing the admission screening. [source:2] You give first, second and third choices. [source:2] About 2 months before enrolment you are told which one could be reserved. [source:2] Cancelling after that costs a cancellation fee. [source:2] The dormitory invoice arrives with the tuition invoice after your Certificate of Eligibility is issued, and the arrangement completes when you pay. [source:2]

Three things follow, and none of them are about money.

You commit before you have seen the room, the building or the neighbourhood. You commit before you know your class timetable, which determines what commute actually costs you in sleep. And you commit at a point when you cannot yet compare it against a real apartment, because you have not got one.

You cannot rent on day one, structurally

This is the part that settles the argument for most first-year students, and it has nothing to do with preference.

At most ports of entry, your residence card is handed to you on arrival. [source:3] At others, your passport is annotated to say the card will be issued later, and it is then issued after you register your address at the municipal office and posted to that address. [source:3]

Read that loop carefully. On that second route, the card goes to the address you register. To register an address, you need an address. So you need somewhere to live before you have the document that most institutions will ask you for.

You also have 14 days from deciding your address to report it. [source:3] A fortnight is not long enough to view flats, negotiate, and complete a tenancy in a country you landed in last week, in a language you are there to learn.

None of this makes renting impossible. It makes renting-from-day-one a thing that needs somebody already in Japan acting for you, or a temporary place to stay while you arrange it. If you have neither, the dormitory is not the conservative option — it is the only one that exists.

What the dormitory actually costs, where it is published

One school publishes figures. Rent from 40,000 to 60,000 yen per month, with utilities charged separately on usage at a guide figure of 5,000 to 10,000 yen per month. [source:1] Dormitories sit 5 to 40 minutes from the campus, around 30 buildings in total, all within 40 minutes door to door. [source:1]

The Sendagaya group publishes no prices at all — there is no fee page on the site. [source:2] So on that option you cannot do the arithmetic before contacting them, and any number you find quoted elsewhere did not come from the school.

That asymmetry is itself a finding. If one school publishes a range and another publishes nothing, the comparison you can actually make before applying is narrower than it looks.

What you give up in a dormitory

You are allocated, not choosing. One school states openly that you may be assigned a dormitory other than your preference. [source:1] With around 30 buildings spread 5 to 40 minutes from campus, the difference between your first choice and your third is a real difference in daily life. [source:1]

Conditions attach to specific buildings. In the Sendagaya listing, some dormitories are men-only, one of those pairs the men-only rule with a meal-plan option, and another runs on meal tickets. [source:2] So "a dormitory place" is not one product.

Things you assume are included may not be. Bedding is not in the room at one school; a futon set can be ordered in advance and you supply the covers. [source:1] Assume nothing is there until the school says it is.

What you give up renting

We are not going to put figures on this side. The costs that make Japanese renting expensive up front are set by landlords and agencies, not by schools, and we have no official source for them — so quoting a range would mean passing on somebody else's estimate as though we had checked it.

What we can say is which questions decide it: whether you need a guarantor and who that can be, what is payable before you get the keys as opposed to monthly, and whether the contract can be signed before you hold a residence card. Those three answers vary enough that a figure from a blog tells you very little about your own case.

Ask your school. They place students in the same few areas every term and they know what landlords near them currently ask of a first-year student with no credit history in Japan.

The sequence most people should use

  • Year one: dormitory, if the school runs one, unless you already have someone in Japan who can sign and search for you. It covers the window when you cannot rent and cannot yet verify anything.
  • Decide early, not well. The allocation runs about 2 months before enrolment, and declining later costs a fee. [source:2] You will be deciding on incomplete information either way — so decide on time and keep the money.
  • Ask what is included before you pay, because the invoice comes with the tuition invoice and after that you are committed. [source:2] Utilities and bedding are the two that catch people. [source:1]
  • Move out in year two, when you have a residence card, a registered address, a timetable you understand and a neighbourhood you have actually walked around.

For which schools run dormitories and what allocation looks like, see the schools that provide dormitories. For the arrival paperwork this all depends on, and the order it has to happen in, see your first week in Japan.

Rents, availability and allocation procedures are set by the schools and change; the pages linked below are the authority. We prepare and forward application documents — accommodation contracts and all payments are between you and the school or the landlord.

claims_without_sources: 自己賃貸の初期費用（敷金・礼金・仲介手数料・保証会社費用）の相場 —— 校方官網からは取れず、入管庁の出典にも当然ない。本文でも金額を書かず、「金額を書かない理由」を明示した。ユーザー指示（具体的な数字は学校官网に出典がある場合のみ）に沿う。
保証人・保証会社の要否 —— 物件と貸主によって異なり、一次資料がない。「どの問いが結論を決めるか」だけ示した。
在留カードなしで賃貸契約が可能かどうか —— 実務上は物件次第であり、公的な出典がない。断定せず問いとして置いた。
「1年目は寮、2年目に移る」という推奨 —— 出典のある事実（寮の割当時期・在留カードの交付経路・14日の届出期限）からの当方の結論であって、学校や官庁の推奨ではない。出典マーカーを付けていないのはそのため。
寮と自己賃貸の総額比較 —— 片側に出典のある数字があり、もう片側にないため、比較そのものを行っていない。片側だけ数字を出して並べると、ない側を読者が勝手に埋めてしまう。
男子限定寮の棟数 —— 一覧から自分で数えた数であり学校の公表値ではない。綴り字（two）で書けば闸门の数字検査に掛からないが、掛からないことは書いてよい理由ではない。「some」に改めた。
